citation.title: Randomization-based confidence sets for the local average treatment effect

standing_assumptions: [Units, potential outcomes, compliance: main p. 3 (PDF p. 3), Section 2.1] We consider an experiment with $n$ units, where each unit is randomized to treatment or control. Let $y_i(d, z)$ denote the potential outcome of unit $i$ under the potential compliance decision $d \in \{0, 1\}$ and the treatment assignment $z \in \{0, 1\}$. Let $d_i(z)$ denote the compliance decision of the $i$th unit when under treatment status $z$. We write $d_i(1) = 0$ if the $i$th unit is assigned to treatment, but does not receive treatment, and write $d_i(1) = 1$ if it does. The compliance decision $d_i(0)$ under assignment to control is defined analogously. [...] Let $[n] = \{1, \ldots, n\}$. Assumption 1 (Exclusion restriction). For all $i \in [n]$, $y_i(d, z)$ is independent of $z$. This assumption implies that treatment assignment affects outcomes only through treatment receipt, and hence $y_i(d, 1) = y_i(d, 0)$ for all $i \in [n]$. Given this assumption, we write $y_i(d)$ from now on to denote the potential outcome under treatment status $d$. [main p. 4 (PDF p. 4)] Assumption 2 (Monotonicity). For all $i \in [n]$, we have $d_i(1) \ge d_i(0)$. Let $\mathcal{C}$ denote the set of compliers, $\mathcal{C} = \{i \in [n] : d_i(0) = 0,\ d_i(1) = 1\}$. (1) Our inferential target is the LATE in the experimental sample, defined by $\bar\beta = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{C}|}\sum_{i \in \mathcal{C}}\{y_i(1) - y_i(0)\}$. (2) We assume throughout the paper that there is at least one complier ($|\mathcal{C}| \ge 1$) so that the quantity is well-defined. [Design and data: main p. 4, Section 2.2] We assume that the experiments under consideration are completely randomized: among $n$ units, researchers assign $n_1$ units to treatment, chosen uniformly at random. [...] For each unit $i$, we let $Z_i$ be a random variable such that $Z_i = 1$ if unit $i$ is assigned to treatment and $Z_i = 0$ otherwise. By definition, $\mathrm{pr}(Z_i = 1) = n_1/n$, and we introduce the shorthand $\pi = n_1/n$. For each unit $i$, researchers observe compliance decisions $D_i = d_i(Z_i)$ and outcomes $Y_i = y_i(D_i)$. Each unit $i$ may additionally be associated with some covariate information [...]; if so, this information is collected in a column vector $x_i \in \mathbb{R}^k$. Throughout the paper we assume that $k$ does not change with the sample size $n$. [...] We adopt the finite-population (design-based) framework, treating the potential outcomes and compliance decisions as fixed parameters [...]. The sole source of randomness in our model is the vector of random treatment assignments, and statistical uncertainties are evaluated exclusively with respect to this randomness. [Studentized statistic: main pp. 4-5, Section 3.1] For all $\beta \in \mathbb{R}$, we define the statistic $\hat\tau(\beta) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n (Y_i - \beta D_i)(Z_i - \pi)$. [...] A short calculation shows that $\hat\tau(\beta) = \pi(1-\pi)\left\{\frac{1}{n_1}\sum_{i=1}^n Z_i(Y_i - \beta D_i) - \frac{1}{n_0}\sum_{i=1}^n (1 - Z_i)(Y_i - \beta D_i)\right\}$, where $n_0 = n - n_1$ [...]. We further define $\hat v_i(1, \beta) = Y_i - \beta D_i - \frac{1}{n_1}\sum_{j=1}^n Z_j(Y_j - \beta D_j)$, $\hat v_i(0, \beta) = Y_i - \beta D_i - \frac{1}{n_0}\sum_{j=1}^n (1 - Z_j)(Y_j - \beta D_j)$. (3) Using this notation, we define the variance estimator $\hat\sigma^2(\beta) = \frac{\pi^2(1-\pi)^2}{n_1^2}\sum_{i=1}^n Z_i\hat v_i^2(1, \beta) + \frac{\pi^2(1-\pi)^2}{n_0^2}\sum_{i=1}^n (1 - Z_i)\hat v_i^2(0, \beta)$ and the studentized statistic $\Delta(\beta) = \frac{\hat\tau(\beta)}{\hat\sigma(\beta)}$. (4) We will use the absolute value $|\Delta(\beta)|$ as our test statistic and construct confidence sets by test inversion. We refer to the test statistic $\Delta(\beta)$ in (4) as the AR statistic. [Randomization distribution and confidence set: main pp. 5-6, Section 3.2] The assignment vector $Z = (Z_1, \ldots, Z_n)$ is a random vector in $\{0, 1\}^n$. Let $Z^*$ be a random vector with the same distribution as $Z$ and which is independent of $Z$. We use $\mathbb{P}^*$ to denote the conditional (on $Z$) probability measure induced by $Z^*$. We define $\hat\tau^* : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ by $\hat\tau^*(\beta) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n (Y_i - \beta D_i)(Z_i^* - \pi)$, where we recall that by definition $Y_i$ and $D_i$ depend only on $Z_i$ and not on $Z_i^*$. We also define the variance estimator $\hat\sigma^{*2}(\beta) = \frac{\pi^2(1-\pi)^2}{n_1^2}\sum_{i=1}^n Z_i^*\left\{Y_i - \beta D_i - \frac{1}{n_1}\sum_{i=1}^n Z_i^*(Y_i - \beta D_i)\right\}^2 + \frac{\pi^2(1-\pi)^2}{n_0^2}\sum_{i=1}^n (1 - Z_i^*)\left\{Y_i - \beta D_i - \frac{1}{n_0}\sum_{i=1}^n (1 - Z_i^*)(Y_i - \beta D_i)\right\}^2$ [the inner sums are the reassigned-arm means; the paper reuses the index $i$] and the studentized statistic $\Delta^*(\beta) = \frac{\hat\tau^*(\beta)}{\hat\sigma^*(\beta)}$. (5) The distribution of $|\Delta^*(\beta)|$ under $\mathbb{P}^*$ is discrete and supported on $[0, \infty]$. For every $\alpha \in (0, 1)$, there exists a smallest (possibly infinite) value $\eta^*_{1-\alpha}(\beta, Z)$ such that $\mathbb{P}^*\{|\Delta^*(\beta)| \le \eta^*_{1-\alpha}(\beta, Z)\} \ge 1 - \alpha$. (6) Our confidence set is defined as $I^*_{1-\alpha}(Z) = \{\beta \in \mathbb{R} : |\Delta(\beta)| \le \eta^*_{1-\alpha}(\beta, Z)\}$. (7) [Assumptions 3 and 4, parameter space $\Theta_n$: main pp. 6-8] Assumption 3 (Parameter space). Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and constants $\delta < 1$ and $A > 0$ be given. Set $w_i(1) = y_i\{d_i(1)\} - \bar\beta d_i(1)$, $w_i(0) = y_i\{d_i(0)\} - \bar\beta d_i(0)$. The following conditions on the potential outcomes and compliance decisions hold. (i) For the given $\delta$, $\sigma_{w(1),w(0),\mathcal{C}} \ge -\delta\,\sigma_{w(1),\mathcal{C}}\,\sigma_{w(0),\mathcal{C}}$. Here, $\sigma_{w(1),w(0),\mathcal{C}}$ is the complier-group covariance of adjusted potential outcomes, $\sigma_{w(1),w(0),\mathcal{C}} = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{C}| - 1}\sum_{i \in \mathcal{C}}\{w_i(1) - \mu_{w(1),\mathcal{C}}\}\{w_i(0) - \mu_{w(0),\mathcal{C}}\}$, where $\mu_{w(a),\mathcal{C}} = |\mathcal{C}|^{-1}\sum_{i \in \mathcal{C}} w_i(a)$ for $a \in \{0, 1\}$, and $\sigma^2_{w(1),\mathcal{C}}$ and $\sigma^2_{w(0),\mathcal{C}}$ are the complier-group potential outcome variances, $\sigma^2_{w(a),\mathcal{C}} = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{C}| - 1}\sum_{i \in \mathcal{C}}\{w_i(a) - \mu_{w(a),\mathcal{C}}\}^2$ for $a \in \{0, 1\}$. If $|\mathcal{C}| = 1$, all variances and covariances are defined to be zero. (ii) For each $a \in \{0, 1\}$ and the given $A$, $\left\{\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n |w_i(a) - \mu_{w(a)}|^4\right\}^{1/4} \le A\sigma_{w(a)}$, where $\mu_{w(a)} = n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n w_i(a)$ and $\sigma^2_{w(a)} = (n-1)^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n \{w_i(a) - \mu_{w(a)}\}^2$. [...] Assumption 4 (Completely randomized experiment). Given $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and a constant $0 < r \le 1/2$, we have $n_1 \in [rn, (1-r)n]$. We denote the parameter space of potential outcomes, compliance decisions and experimental designs satisfying Assumptions 1-4 with $n$ units and constants $\delta$, $r$ and $A$ by $\Theta_n(\delta, r, A) = \left\{\left(\{(y_i(1), y_i(0), d_i(1), d_i(0))\}_{i=1}^n, \Pi_n\right)\right\}$, where $\{(y_i(1), y_i(0), d_i(1), d_i(0))\}_{i=1}^n$ satisfies Assumption 3 with constants $\delta$ and $A$, and $\Pi_n$ is a distribution of random assignment variables $\{Z_i\}_{i=1}^n$ implementing complete randomization that satisfies Assumption 4 with constant $r$. Each combination of potential outcomes, compliance decisions and an experimental design completely determines the distribution of our test statistic. [...] For each parameter $\theta$ in the parameter space, we denote its LATE by $\bar\beta(\theta)$. [Regression adjustment: main pp. 8-10, Sections 4.1-4.3] [...] each unit $i$ comes equipped with a column vector $x_i \in \mathbb{R}^k$ of covariates for some $k \in \mathbb{N}$. We suppose that each $x_i$ is demeaned, meaning that $\sum_{i=1}^n x_i = 0_k$, where $0_k$ denotes the zero vector in $\mathbb{R}^k$. [...] We denote the $s$th element of $x_i$ by $x_{si}$. Given a $\beta \in \mathbb{R}$ and a treatment assignment vector $Z$, consider the linear regression $Y_i - \beta D_i \sim (1 - Z_i)\varphi_0 + Z_i\varphi_1 + (1 - Z_i)x_i'\gamma_0 + Z_i x_i'\gamma_1$. (8) This is an interacted linear regression that regresses $Y_i - \beta D_i$ on $((1 - Z_i), Z_i, (1 - Z_i)x_i, Z_i x_i)$ without an intercept. For each $\beta$, denote the ordinary least squares (OLS) estimators resulting from (8) by $\hat\varphi(0, \beta)$, $\hat\varphi(1, \beta)$, $\hat\gamma(0, \beta)$ and $\hat\gamma(1, \beta)$, corresponding to the order in which the associated coefficients appear in (8). We define the randomization statistics $\hat\varphi^*(0, \beta)$, $\hat\varphi^*(1, \beta)$, $\hat\gamma^*(0, \beta)$ and $\hat\gamma^*(1, \beta)$ similarly by using $Z^*$ instead of $Z$. [main p. 9] We define the covariate-adjusted difference-in-means statistic as $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{adj}}(\beta) = \frac{1}{n_1}\sum_{i=1}^n Z_i\{Y_i - \beta D_i - x_i'\hat\gamma(1, \beta)\} - \frac{1}{n_0}\sum_{i=1}^n (1 - Z_i)\{Y_i - \beta D_i - x_i'\hat\gamma(0, \beta)\}$, (9) and we define the covariate-adjusted randomization estimator $\hat\tau^*_{\mathrm{adj}}(\beta)$ analogously, again replacing $Z_i$ by $Z_i^*$ and replacing $\hat\gamma(0, \beta)$ and $\hat\gamma(1, \beta)$ by their randomization analogues. [...] The residual estimators associated with (8) and their randomization-based counterparts are $\hat\varepsilon_i(\beta) = Y_i - \beta D_i - \hat\varphi(Z_i, \beta) - x_i'\hat\gamma(Z_i, \beta)$, $\hat\varepsilon_i^*(\beta) = Y_i - \beta D_i - \hat\varphi^*(Z_i^*, \beta) - x_i'\hat\gamma^*(Z_i^*, \beta)$. We use these to define the variance estimators $\hat\sigma^2_{\mathrm{adj}}(\beta) = \frac{1}{n_1^2}\sum_{i=1}^n Z_i\hat\varepsilon_i(\beta)^2 + \frac{1}{n_0^2}\sum_{i=1}^n (1 - Z_i)\hat\varepsilon_i(\beta)^2$, $\hat\sigma^{2*}_{\mathrm{adj}}(\beta) = \frac{1}{n_1^2}\sum_{i=1}^n Z_i^*\hat\varepsilon_i^*(\beta)^2 + \frac{1}{n_0^2}\sum_{i=1}^n (1 - Z_i^*)\hat\varepsilon_i^*(\beta)^2$. The adjusted studentized difference-in-means statistics are then $\Delta_{\mathrm{adj}}(\beta) = \frac{\hat\tau_{\mathrm{adj}}(\beta)}{\hat\sigma_{\mathrm{adj}}(\beta)}$, $\Delta^*_{\mathrm{adj}}(\beta) = \frac{\hat\tau^*_{\mathrm{adj}}(\beta)}{\hat\sigma^*_{\mathrm{adj}}(\beta)}$. (10) [...] Given $\alpha \in (0, 1)$, there exists a smallest (possibly infinite) value $\eta^{\mathrm{adj},*}_{1-\alpha}(\beta, Z)$ such that $\mathbb{P}^*\{|\Delta^*_{\mathrm{adj}}(\beta)| \le \eta^{\mathrm{adj},*}_{1-\alpha}(\beta, Z)\} \ge 1 - \alpha$. [main p. 10] Our proposed confidence set is $I^{\mathrm{adj},*}_{1-\alpha}(Z) = \{\beta \in \mathbb{R} : |\Delta_{\mathrm{adj}}(\beta)| \le \eta^{\mathrm{adj},*}_{1-\alpha}(\beta, Z)\}$. (11) [Assumption 5 and parameter space $\Xi_n$: main pp. 10-11] Assumption 5. Let $k, n \in \mathbb{N}$ and constants $\delta < 1$ and $\tilde\varepsilon, A, B > 0$ be given. For each $a \in \{0, 1\}$, define $\varepsilon_i(a, \bar\beta) = y_i\{d_i(a)\} - \bar\beta d_i(a) - \varphi(a, \bar\beta) - x_i'\gamma(a, \bar\beta)$. The following conditions on the potential outcomes, compliance decisions and covariates hold. (i) For the given $\delta$, $\sigma_{\varepsilon(1,\bar\beta),\varepsilon(0,\bar\beta)} \ge -\delta\sigma_{\varepsilon(1,\bar\beta)}\sigma_{\varepsilon(0,\bar\beta)}$. (ii) For each $a \in \{0, 1\}$ and the given $B$, $\left\{\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \varepsilon_i^4(a, \bar\beta)\right\}^{1/4} \le B\sigma_{\varepsilon(a,\bar\beta)}$. (iii) We have that $\sum_{i=1}^n x_i = 0_k$. (iv) For all $s \in [k]$ and the given $A$, we have that $n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n x_{si}^4 \le A$. (v) Let $\lambda_{\min}$ denote the smallest eigenvalue of $n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n x_i x_i'$. Then for the given $\tilde\varepsilon$, $\lambda_{\min} \ge \tilde\varepsilon$. We denote the parameter space of potential outcomes, compliance decisions, covariates and experimental designs satisfying Assumptions 1, 2, 4 and 5 with $n$ units, covariates of dimension $k$, and constants $\delta$, $\tilde\varepsilon$, $A$, $B$ and $r$ by $\Xi_n(k, \delta, \tilde\varepsilon, A, B, r) = \left\{\left(\{(y_i(1), y_i(0), d_i(1), d_i(0), x_i)\}_{i=1}^n, \Pi_n\right)\right\}$. Here, $\{(y_i(1), y_i(0), d_i(1), d_i(0), x_i)\}_{i=1}^n$ satisfies Assumption 5 with constants $\delta$, $\tilde\varepsilon$, $A$ and $B$, and $\Pi_n$ is a distribution of random assignment variables $\{Z_i\}_{i=1}^n$ implementing complete randomization that satisfies Assumption 4 with constant $r$. [The population variances and covariance in Assumption 5 are those of Supplement A.1 below, with divisor $n - 1$; $\varphi(a, \beta)$, $\gamma(a, \beta)$ are defined in Supplement D.2 below.] [Supplement A, notation: Supplement p. 21 (Supplement PDF p. 1)] We let $\mathbb{N}$ denote the positive integers [...]. We use the notation $\lesssim$ to denote inequalities that hold up to a constant independent of $n$. [...] We also define a set $\mathcal{A}$ of always-takers and a set $\mathcal{N}$ of never-takers by $\mathcal{A} = \{i \in [n] : d_i(0) = 1, d_i(1) = 1\}$, $\mathcal{N} = \{i \in [n] : d_i(0) = 0, d_i(1) = 0\}$. Let $\mathcal{T}(1), \mathcal{T}(0) \subset [n]$ denote the sets of subjects in the treatment and control groups defined by $Z$, respectively, so that $\mathcal{T}(1) = \{i \in [n] : Z_i = 1\}$, $\mathcal{T}(0) = \{i \in [n] : Z_i = 0\}$. Given a vector $v$, we use $\|v\|_2$ to denote the standard $l_2$ vector norm. [...] A.1. For any vector $q = (q_i)_{i=1}^n \in \mathbb{R}^n$, we define the population mean and variance by $\mu_q = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n q_i$, $\sigma_q^2 = \frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n (q_i - \mu_q)^2$. We also define within-group variances for each group $G \in \{\mathcal{A}, \mathcal{C}, \mathcal{N}\}$ by $\sigma^2_{q,G} = \frac{1}{|G| - 1}\sum_{i \in G}(q_i - \mu_{q,G})^2$, where $\mu_{q,G} = \frac{1}{|G|}\sum_{i \in G} q_i$ if $|G| \ge 2$ and zero otherwise. Given an additional vector $\tilde q = (\tilde q_i)_{i=1}^n \in \mathbb{R}^n$, we define the population covariance by $\sigma_{q\tilde q} = \frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n (q_i - \mu_q)(\tilde q_i - \mu_{\tilde q})$, and the within-group covariances by $\sigma_{q\tilde q,G} = \frac{1}{|G| - 1}\sum_{i \in G}(q_i - \mu_{q,G})(\tilde q_i - \mu_{\tilde q,G})$, if $|G| \ge 2$ and zero otherwise. A.2. Let $\mathcal{Z}$ be a mean zero, variance one normal random variable. [...] For an $\alpha \in (0, 1)$, define $z_{1-\alpha} \in \mathbb{R}$ as the value such that $\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{Z} > z_{1-\alpha}) = \alpha$. [Supplement B.1 and B.3: Supplement p. 22 (PDF p. 2)] Lemma 2. For all $\beta \in \mathbb{R}$, the variance of $\hat\tau(\beta)$ is $\operatorname{var}(\hat\tau(\beta)) = \frac{S_1^2(\beta)}{n_1} + \frac{S_0^2(\beta)}{n_0} - \frac{S_{10}^2(\beta)}{n}$, (B.1) where $S_1^2(\beta) = \frac{\pi^2(1-\pi)^2}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n v_i(1, \beta)^2$, $S_0^2(\beta) = \frac{\pi^2(1-\pi)^2}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n v_i(0, \beta)^2$, $S_{10}^2(\beta) = \frac{\pi^2(1-\pi)^2}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n (v_i(1, \beta) - v_i(0, \beta))^2$, (B.2) $v_i(1, \beta) = y_i(d_i(1)) - \beta d_i(1) - \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n (y_i(d_i(1)) - \beta d_i(1))$, (B.3) $v_i(0, \beta) = y_i(d_i(0)) - \beta d_i(0) - \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n (y_i(d_i(0)) - \beta d_i(0))$. (B.4) [...] Lemma 3. We have $E[\hat\tau(\beta)] = 0$ when $\beta = |\mathcal{C}|^{-1}\sum_{i \in \mathcal{C}}(y_i(1) - y_i(0))$. [Supplement C, conventions: Supplement p. 23 (PDF p. 3)] Throughout this section, we let $\delta, r, A$ be the constants fixed in the statement of Theorem 1, and set $\Theta_n = \Theta_n(\delta, r, A)$. The notation $\Theta_n$ encodes Assumptions 1-4. We typically denote elements of $\Theta_n$ by $\theta_n$. For each model $\theta_n$, we denote its local average treatment effect by $\bar\beta(\theta_n)$ [...]. In various lemmas below, we will consider subsequences $(\theta_{n_k})_{k=1}^\infty$ of a given sequence $(\theta_n)_{n=1}^\infty$ of models. We let $n_{1k}$ denote the number of elements in the treatment group of $\theta_{n_k}$, and $n_{0k}$ the number of elements in the control group of $\theta_{n_k}$, so that $n_{0k} + n_{1k} = n_k$. [...] For the remainder of the proofs, we will implicitly assume that the variances $\sigma^2_{w(a)}$, for $a \in \{0, 1\}$ as defined in Assumption 3, are both strictly positive. This entails no loss of generality provided we adopt the convention that $0/0 = 0$. If both variances are zero, then the complier treatment effect is constant and additive, so the exact coverage result of the randomization-based CI in Imbens & Rosenbaum (2005) applies. [...] Similar comments apply to the proofs in Section D. [...] In results on sequences $(\theta_n)_{n=1}^\infty$, we will generally omit the $n$-dependence on $w_i(1)$, $w_i(0)$, and other model-dependent quantities for brevity. [Supplement C.3: Supplement pp. 27-28 (PDF pp. 7-8)] We write $E^*$ and $\operatorname{var}^*$ for expectation and variance under the probability measure $\mathbb{P}^*$. By Lemma 3, for any $\beta$ we have $E^*[\hat\tau^*(\beta)] = 0$, and by Lemma 2, $\operatorname{var}^*(\hat\tau^*(\beta)) = \frac{S_1^{*2}(\beta)}{n_1} + \frac{S_0^{*2}(\beta)}{n_0}$, (C.25) where $S_1^{*2}(\beta) = S_0^{*2}(\beta) = \frac{\pi^2(1-\pi)^2}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n \left(Y_i - \beta D_i - \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n (Y_i - \beta D_i)\right)^2$. (C.26) [...] We recall that $\mu_Y = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n Y_i$, $\mu_D = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n D_i$ and define $\hat\mu_{y(d(a))} = \frac{1}{n_a}\sum_{i \in \mathcal{T}(a)} y_i(d_i(a))$, $\hat\mu_{d(a)} = \frac{1}{n_a}\sum_{i \in \mathcal{T}(a)} d_i(a)$, for each $a \in \{0, 1\}$. [Supplement D, least-squares parameters and infeasible estimator: Supplement pp. 31-32 (PDF pp. 11-12)] We let $k, \delta, \tilde\varepsilon, A, B, r$ be the constants fixed in the statement of Theorem 2, and set $\Xi_n = \Xi_n(k, \delta, \tilde\varepsilon, A, B, r)$. D.2. Suppose a $\beta \in \mathbb{R}$ is given. Then we define, for each $a \in \{0, 1\}$, outcomes $w_i(a, \beta)$ by $w_i(a, \beta) = y_i(d_i(a)) - \beta d_i(a)$. (D.1) We define the least-squares regression parameters $\varphi(a, \beta) : \{0, 1\} \times \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$, $\gamma(a, \beta) : \{0, 1\} \times \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}^k$, by $(\varphi(a, \beta), \gamma(a, \beta)) = \arg\min_{(s,t) \in \mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R}^k}\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n (w_i(a, \beta) - s - x_i't)^2$, (D.2) where we interpret $t$ as a column vector. We define the residuals for (D.2) by $\varepsilon_i(a, \beta) = w_i(a, \beta) - \varphi(a, \beta) - x_i'\gamma(a, \beta)$. The parameters $\varphi^*(a, \beta)$ and $\gamma^*(a, \beta)$ are defined similarly, by replacing $w_i(a, \beta)$ with $Y_i - \beta D_i$ in (D.2), and we define the associated residuals $\varepsilon_i^*(\beta)$ by $\varepsilon_i^*(\beta) = Y_i - \beta D_i - \varphi^*(a, \beta) - x_i'\gamma^*(a, \beta)$. (D.3) These definitions imply that $\varphi^*(0, \beta) = \varphi^*(1, \beta)$ and $\gamma^*(0, \beta) = \gamma^*(1, \beta)$. D.3. To analyze the asymptotic behavior of $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{adj}}(\beta)$, we define the infeasible estimator $\tilde\tau_{\mathrm{adj}}(\beta) = \frac{1}{n_1}\sum_{i=1}^n Z_i(Y_i - \beta D_i - x_i'\gamma(1, \beta)) - \frac{1}{n_0}\sum_{i=1}^n (1 - Z_i)(Y_i - \beta D_i - x_i'\gamma(0, \beta))$. (D.4) The infeasible estimator $\tilde\tau^*_{\mathrm{adj}}(\beta)$ is defined similarly, replacing $Z_i$ by $Z_i^*$, and $\gamma(1, \beta)$ and $\gamma(0, \beta)$ by $\gamma^*(1, \beta)$ and $\gamma^*(0, \beta)$, respectively. A straightforward adaptation of Lemma 2 shows that $\operatorname{var}(\tilde\tau_{\mathrm{adj}}(\beta)) = \frac{\mathcal{S}_1^2(\beta)}{n_1} + \frac{\mathcal{S}_0^2(\beta)}{n_0} - \frac{\mathcal{S}_{10}^2(\beta)}{n}$, (D.5) where $\mathcal{S}_1^2(\beta) = \frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n \varepsilon_i^2(1, \beta)$, $\mathcal{S}_0^2(\beta) = \frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n \varepsilon_i^2(0, \beta)$, $\mathcal{S}_{10}^2(\beta) = \frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n (\varepsilon_i(1, \beta) - \varepsilon_i(0, \beta))^2$. Similarly, $\operatorname{var}^*(\tilde\tau^*_{\mathrm{adj}}(\beta)) = \frac{\mathcal{S}_{1,*}^2(\beta)}{n_1} + \frac{\mathcal{S}_{0,*}^2(\beta)}{n_0}$, $\mathcal{S}_{1,*}^2(\beta) = \mathcal{S}_{0,*}^2(\beta) = \frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n \varepsilon_i^*(\beta)^2$. (D.6) [Supplement E.1: Supplement p. 32 (PDF p. 12)] Denote $x_i^\circ = [0, x_i']' \in \mathbb{R}^{k+1}$ and $\tilde x_i = [1, x_i']' \in \mathbb{R}^{k+1}$. For $a \in \{0, 1\}$, define $\psi(a, \beta) = \begin{bmatrix}\varphi(a, \beta) \\ \gamma(a, \beta)\end{bmatrix}$, $\hat\psi(a, \beta) = \begin{bmatrix}\hat\varphi(a, \beta) \\ \hat\gamma(a, \beta)\end{bmatrix}$. (E.1) We denote their randomization counterparts as $\psi^*(a, \beta)$ and $\hat\psi^*(a, \beta)$. Lemma 14. The following claims hold. 1. canonical_claim.statement: Lemma 20. Fix $k\in\mathbb N$ with $k\ge1$, $\delta\in\mathbb R$ with $\delta<1$, $\tilde\varepsilon,A,B>0$ and $r\in(0,1/2]$. Let $(N_j)_{j\in\mathbb N}$ be a strictly increasing sequence of population sizes with $N_j\ge2$, and let $(\theta_{N_j})_{j\in\mathbb N}$ be a deterministic sequence of models with covariates such that $\theta_{N_j}\in\Xi_{N_j}(k,\delta,\tilde\varepsilon,A,B,r)$ for every $j$. Denote $\beta_{N_j}=\bar\beta(\theta_{N_j})$. Assume additionally that $\sigma^2_{\varepsilon(a,\beta_{N_j})}(\theta_{N_j})>0$ for every $j\in\mathbb N$ and both $a\in\{0,1\}$, where these are the variances of the population OLS regression residuals, not the variances of the unprojected adjusted outcomes. Let $(\theta_{n_\ell})_{\ell\in\mathbb N}$ be any fixed subsequence, with $n_\ell=N_{s(\ell)}$ for a strictly increasing map $s:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N$. The following four claims hold on one event of probability one with respect to the randomness in the observed assignments $Z$, simultaneously for all the positive thresholds appearing below. 1. For every $\kappa > 0$, $\lim_{\ell\to\infty}\mathbb{P}^*\left(\left|\hat\tau^*_{\mathrm{adj}}(\beta_{n_\ell}) - \tilde\tau^*_{\mathrm{adj}}(\beta_{n_\ell})\right| \ge \kappa\sqrt{\operatorname{var}^*\left(\tilde\tau^*_{\mathrm{adj}}(\beta_{n_\ell})\right)}\right) = 0$. (E.58) 2. For every $x > 0$, $\lim_{\ell\to\infty}\left|\mathbb{P}^*\left(\left|\tilde\tau^*_{\mathrm{adj}}(\beta_{n_\ell})\right| \ge x\sqrt{\operatorname{var}^*\left(\tilde\tau^*_{\mathrm{adj}}(\beta_{n_\ell})\right)}\right) - \mathbb{P}(|\mathcal{Z}| \ge x)\right| = 0$. (E.59) 3. For every $x > 0$, $\lim_{\ell\to\infty}\left|\mathbb{P}^*\left(\left|\hat\tau^*_{\mathrm{adj}}(\beta_{n_\ell})\right| \ge x\sqrt{\operatorname{var}^*\left(\tilde\tau^*_{\mathrm{adj}}(\beta_{n_\ell})\right)}\right) - \mathbb{P}(|\mathcal{Z}| \ge x)\right| = 0$. (E.60) 4. For every $\kappa > 0$, $\lim_{\ell\to\infty}\mathbb{P}^*\left(\left|\frac{\hat\sigma^2_{\mathrm{adj},*}(\beta_{n_\ell})}{\operatorname{var}^*\left(\tilde\tau^*_{\mathrm{adj}}(\beta_{n_\ell})\right)} - 1\right| \ge \kappa\right) = 0$. (E.61, corrected: the denominator is the randomization variance of the infeasible statistic $\tilde\tau^*_{\mathrm{adj}}$, as in (E.58)-(E.60) and (D.6); the positive population residual-variance hypothesis above is an additional qualification of all four limits.)

The newly required population residual variances are $\sigma^2_{\varepsilon(a,\beta)}(\theta)=(n-1)^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n\varepsilon_i(a,\beta)^2$, where $\varepsilon_i(a,\beta)=y_i(d_i(a))-\beta d_i(a)-(1,x_i')\psi(a,\beta)$ and $\psi(a,\beta)$ is the population OLS coefficient vector including an intercept (D.2); the residual mean is zero. Strict positivity is required separately for $a=0$ and $a=1$ at each size used, with no uniform positive lower bound in the sample size. All constants are fixed along the sequence. Each observed assignment $Z_{N_j}$ is a measurable random variable on a common probability space and has exactly the complete-randomization law for $\theta_{N_j}$; any joint coupling of these marginals is allowed. At each size $Z^*$ is a fresh draw from that same law, independent of the observed assignments, with the observed response vector held fixed. On a rank-deficient arm, use one fixed measurable choice of a least-squares minimizer, agreeing with the unique normal-equations solution on full-rank arms. canonical_claim.note:
The denominator repair in (E.61) is retained: it is the reassignment variance of the pooled-coefficient oracle $\tilde\tau^*_{\mathrm{adj}}$, not of the statistic that re-estimates the arm regressions. The audit's former one-symbol repair was insufficient for its unqualified four-claim statement; the qualified version here additionally restricts to strictly positive population OLS residual variances in both arms. This is an explicit additional hypothesis, even when the unprojected $w(a,\beta_n)$ variances are positive. It is not a change to the test statistic or the confidence set.

Check of falsity without this hypothesis: for every $n\ge2$, set $n_1=\lfloor n/2\rfloor$, make every unit a complier, and set $y_i(0)=y_i(1)=x_i$, with $\lfloor n/2\rfloor$ entries of each sign $-1,+1$ and one additional $0$ at odd sizes. The models belong to $\Xi_n(1,0,1/2,1,1,1/3)$: the covariate mean is zero, its second moment is at least $1/2$, its fourth moment is at most $1$, and both residual schedules vanish. The unprojected variances are $n/(n-1)$ at even sizes and $1$ at odd sizes. The full-population augmented Gram is $\operatorname{diag}(1,\overline{x^2})$, the population and pooled coefficients are $(0,1)$, and the oracle reassignment statistic and variance are zero for every observed assignment. Thus the non-strict event in (E.58) has probability one for every positive threshold, independently of the feasible OLS selection and of division conventions. The same zero scale makes the tail events in (E.59) and (E.60) certain. The growing family therefore refutes the old statement even if sample sizes are required at every integer $n\ge2$, rather than only at even sizes.

Check of the repaired statement: the fixed Xi bounds and the added positivity give almost-sure eventual positivity and a uniform relative fourth-moment bound for the pooled observed residuals.
